Analytical AI is purpose-built to analyse: it takes a business question, reasons through data, structures a conclusion, and cites every source. Generative AI is purpose-built to converse: it predicts the next plausible word from patterns in its training data. Both use large models. They are built for opposite jobs.

Ask a generative model for a market analysis and it drafts fluent prose that sounds authoritative, assembled from probability, not evidence. It can invent a statistic, misattribute a source, or answer confidently on data it never saw. That is not a flaw to patch; it is the job it was built for — conversation, not analysis.

Caspr is Analytical AI. Type a single-line prompt, and Caspr proposes a structured layout, asks the clarifying questions an analyst would ask, then delivers a boardroom-ready PDF or editable PPTX — every insight cited to a credible source, drawn from 25M+ curated documents, government databases, and news feeds. No scraping, no invention.

Three stages do the work. Assessment is the research methodology: it reasons through the data and structures the conclusions, rather than retrieving and paraphrasing snippets. Sourcing is the live data layer: it pulls from real-time feeds, so the analysis reflects today's market, not a training cutoff from months or years ago.

The distinction matters commercially, not just technically. A chatbot gives you a starting point you still have to verify line by line. Caspr gives you a document you can put in front of a board, because you can trace every claim back to its source before anyone in the room asks where the number came from.

That's why consultants, investors, and strategy teams reach for Caspr instead of a chat window when the deliverable is a market sizing, a competitive landscape, or a due-diligence screen. Generative AI is excellent at drafting an email or a first pass at a pitch. It was never built to defend a number in a boardroom — and it shouldn't have to be, because that was never the job.

While the world was building generative AI, we built analytical AI.

See Analytical AI in action.

Assessment is Caspr's research methodology — the stage that reconciles what sources disagree on that turns a question into a structured, defensible answer. Most AI tools retrieve: they search a corpus, pull the closest-matching snippets, and stitch them into a paragraph. Assessment reasons: it works through the data the way a senior analyst would, weighing sources against each other and building toward a conclusion, not just returning what it found first.

In practice, this is what separates a report from a lookup. When you prompt Caspr, the assessment stage proposes a structured layout for the analysis, asks the clarifying questions that sharpen scope, then works through the relevant sources to construct each section's argument — figures, comparisons, and conclusions that follow from the evidence, not just sit beside it. Every insight it produces carries its source, so the reasoning can be checked, not just trusted.

This is why a Caspr report reads like something an analyst wrote, not something a search engine assembled. A market-sizing section doesn't just list numbers pulled from different reports — it reconciles them, flags where sources disagree, and lands on a defensible estimate. A competitive landscape doesn't just describe competitors — it structures them against the dimensions that matter to your question.

Assessment runs on every analysis, from a $15 Brief to a $300 Intelligence report. Deeper depths simply give it more scope to reason through, not a different method.

It's paired with the sourcing stage, Caspr's live data layer, so the reasoning is always applied to current information rather than a fixed, ageing dataset. One structures the argument; the other keeps the facts underneath it current. Neither replaces judgment — both are built so the reader can check the judgment for themselves, source by source.

Watch the assessment stage work.

Sourcing is Caspr's live data layer — the system that keeps every analysis current. A trained model's knowledge is frozen at the point its training data was collected; ask it about this quarter's numbers and it either doesn't know or guesses. Sourcing pulls from real-time feeds, so the analysis reflects today's reality, not a training cutoff.

This matters most exactly when it's least convenient to ignore: a market that moved this quarter, a competitor that just raised a round, a regulation that changed last month. A model trained months ago will describe the market as it stood when that training data was collected. Caspr's sourcing checks against live sources — documents, government databases, news feeds — as the report is built, so the figures and events in your analysis are current, not stale.

Paired with the assessment stage, which structures the reasoning, the sourcing stage supplies the facts to reason with. Together they're why a Caspr report can cite a source published last week as readily as one published last year, and why its conclusions hold up when someone in the room checks them against this morning's news.

For anything time-sensitive — a live deal, a fast-moving category, a board update due this quarter — the sourcing stage is the difference between an analysis that was true and one that still is.

This is also the practical reason Caspr doesn't simply run on a fixed, pre-indexed dataset. A market can shift meaningfully in the weeks between a training run and the day you need an answer. Sourcing is built so that gap never shows up in your report.

Analyse today's data.

Caspr draws on 25M+ curated, credible sources — documents, government databases, and news feeds — not the open web. Every source is selected for credibility before it enters the system, not filtered after the fact.

That distinction is the point. Web scraping pulls whatever a crawler can reach: SEO content farms, unverified blog posts, outdated pages, content written to game search rankings rather than to inform. Feed that into an analysis and you inherit its noise — numbers with no provenance, claims no one stands behind. Caspr's source base is curated the way a research desk builds its library: government statistics agencies, regulatory filings, industry databases, and vetted news, selected because they can be checked.

The result shows up in the report itself. Every insight is shown with the source it came from, so a number in a market-sizing section can be traced back to the filing or database it was pulled from, not to "the internet." That's what makes the output defensible in front of people whose job is to find the weak point in your numbers — an analyst, an investment committee, a board.

Sourcing keeps this source base live, pulling current data as each analysis runs, so a report built today reflects today's filings and this week's news, not a stale index built once and left to age.

Curation also means Caspr doesn't need to guess at reliability the way an open-web system does. A government database or a regulatory filing doesn't need to be cross-checked against ten other pages to be trusted; it's already the primary source. That's the standard applied to every one of the 25M+ sources in the system, across every industry and geography a question might touch.

See how sources are cited.

Every insight in a Caspr report carries a citation. Look for the small red dot beside a claim — a market-size figure, a growth rate, a competitor's revenue — and you're looking at a number with a source attached, not a number that merely sounded right.

Click the dot and Caspr answers you directly, through Ask Caspr, with the specific source behind that specific claim: the document, the database, the report it came from. The citation is scoped to the sentence you clicked, not a general bibliography you have to search.

The full list of every source used sits on its own card at the end of the report — the last page, not a footnote buried mid-paragraph. No numbered references, no separate Sources tab to hunt through. Everything traces back from the claim itself, on demand, without you leaving the page you're reading.

This is what a slide from a boutique consulting deck rarely offers: a number you can defend without calling the analyst who wrote it. Put a Caspr figure in front of your board, and if someone asks where it came from, you already have the answer — click, read, cite it back.

That's the difference between analytical AI and a chatbot's best guess. Generative AI produces a plausible sentence. Caspr produces a sourced one, drawn from 25M+ curated documents, government databases, and news feeds — not open web scraping — and shows its work the moment you ask. The citation isn't decoration. It's why the report survives a room full of people whose job is finding the hole in your numbers.

"Hallucination" is what happens when generative AI writes a plausible-sounding sentence with no fact behind it — a market size, a date, a quote, invented because it fit the pattern of the text. It reads confidently. It can be entirely wrong, and nothing in the sentence itself tells you which.

Caspr avoids this by construction, not by caution. Every insight in a report is generated from a specific, cited source — one of 25M+ curated documents, government databases, and live data feeds. Assessment doesn't compose a sentence and hope it's accurate; it retrieves and reasons from a source, then states the conclusion that source actually supports. There is nothing unsourced left for it to invent, because invention was never part of the process to begin with.

That's why every claim carries a red-dot citation you can click and verify yourself, and why the full source list sits on the report's last page. Zero hallucinations doesn't mean "trust us." It means the architecture leaves no room for a plausible-but-invented number to appear in your report in the first place — there's no step where Caspr is asked to guess.

Name the fear directly: the wrong figure, stated with total confidence, sitting on slide fourteen of a board deck with your name on the cover. Generative AI cannot promise that won't happen — it wasn't built to know the difference between a real number and a convincing one. Caspr was, because every number is traceable before it ever reaches your slide, which means you can check it before anyone else in the room does.

That's the practical difference between generative and analytical AI: one produces plausible text, the other produces defensible conclusions. Don't take our word for it — see the sourcing yourself.

Because scraping optimises for coverage, not credibility. A crawler pulls whatever it can reach — content farms, SEO-written pages, outdated statistics, claims with no author behind them — and an AI system built on that input inherits its noise. Caspr is built the other way round: 25M+ curated sources, selected for credibility before they enter the system, not filtered after.

The sources are documents, government databases, and news feeds — the kind of material a research desk would actually cite, not whatever a search-engine-optimised blog post happens to rank for. Curation is an editorial standard, applied before the analysis runs, so the conclusion is only ever as good as the evidence it's built on, and the evidence has already been vetted.

This is why every insight in a Caspr report carries its source. Not because citation is a nice feature, but because it's the natural output of starting from credible material — when you can trust the input, you can show your work without hoping no one checks it. Scraped, unverified content can't make that promise; there's no way to cite a source responsibly if the source itself was never verified.

For anyone whose numbers get challenged in a room — an analyst, an investment committee, a board — that difference is the whole point of curation over scraping.

It also means Caspr can be honest about scope. A source base built for coverage of every corner of the web can claim to cover everything and verify little of it. A curated source base is more selective by design — and more defensible for exactly that reason. Depth of trust, not breadth of noise, is the trade Caspr makes.

The alternative is the quiet risk in most AI-generated research: a confident answer built on data that was current when the model was trained, not when you asked the question. Caspr closes that gap by design.

Analyse the latest data.

You're left fact-checking every number before you can use it.

Type a single-line prompt, and Caspr proposes a structured layout, asks the clarifying questions an analyst would, then delivers a boardroom-ready, fully-cited PDF or editable PPTX — reasoning through the data with the assessment stage, pulling current data with the sourcing stage, and showing the source behind every insight. Nothing in the report is unsourced, because nothing in the source base is scraped or invented.

The practical test: can you hand the output straight to someone whose job is to find the hole in it? A chat transcript needs verification before it earns that trust. A Caspr report is built to survive it.

This isn't a knock on ChatGPT — it's an excellent tool for what it was built to do: draft, summarise, brainstorm, converse. Research that has to hold up under scrutiny is a different job, with a different bar. Caspr was purpose-built for that bar.
